newsitem.title: USA: UPS seeks court orders against strikers.
newsitem.headline: UPS seeks court orders against strikers.

text.p: United Parcel Service sought court orders in at least nine states to prevent striking workers from blocking delivery trucks and management from reporting to work, officials said Thursday.

A state court in Colorado granted a 10-day temporary restraining order, limiting the number of pickets on the line and preventing striking workers from harassing UPS employees, a court clerk said on Thursday.

The giant parcel delivery company filed for other orders in towns in Massachusetts, where pickets lines have been the most volatile, and in California, Ohio, Colorado, New York and in other states where members of the Teamsters union have interfered with business, a UPS official said.

"Quite frankly in a number of different areas, they have been impeding our ability to do business," UPS spokeswoman Jennifer Jiles told Reuters. "We are not trying to stop them from picketing," she added.
A spokesman for the 185,000 striking members of the Teamsters said UPS should have no difficulty finding a sympathetic judge to issue a restraining order.
"I don't see that as any big deal," said Teamsters spokesman Rand Wilson. "Unfortunately, in many areas of the country, the political and legal system is stacked against workers."
Wilson said the local chapters of the union may try to challenge any court orders which are granted, but UPS has 6,000 locations across the country where Teamsters can strike.
In Colorado, an Adams County judge granted a 10-day restraining order at the UPS operation in Commerce City, located outside Denver.
The order also prohibits pickets from threatening, harassing or intimidating UPS workers and customers of UPS who come into the plant, a court clerk said.

In a motion filed in the U.S. District Court in Boston, UPS said the strikers' "present unlawful acts are causing immediate and irreparable injury to UPS and its employees and customers, have caused physical injury to private citizens and to employees of UPS, and constitute an ongoing, serious and irreparable threat to the public safety."

The motion included the affadavits of the chiefs of police at six Massachusetts communities, stating that nearly 50 strikers have been arrested in recent days and at least two police officers have been injured.
The strike has strained police resources and endangered the public and they therefore supported a temporary restraining order, the affadavits said.

Police Chief Armand Caron of Chelmsford, where 16 arrests have been made, said the injury of two police officers there "reduces my ability to not only protect the public at this facility but also the residents of this town."
"We seem to be having the biggest problems on our picket lines in Massachusetts," UPS spokesman Norman Black said.
U.S. District Judge George O'Toole ordered a court hearing for 11 a.m. EDT (1500 GMT) on Friday in Boston for the proposed restraining order.
